extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers and performers (stand-up, sketch, and TV sitcom writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing jokes using the Rule-of‑Threes: how to set up a clear pattern with the first items and craft an unexpected, connected payoff. Aimed at writers/performers working in stand-up and scripted comedy (sitcoms, sketches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-of-Threes mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule-of-Threes establishes a pattern and then ends with something unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up a recognizable pattern with the first elements, then break that pattern on the third item to create the laugh. Example (lame): “We serve lasagna, spaghetti, and poi.” The device depends on expectation formed by the pattern and a surprising payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two items to establish pattern; third as payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually two items are sufficient to establish the pattern. Three is overkill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You get the pattern with two items; the third functions as the unexpected element. Overlong lists (more than three) often feel wrong because audiences are conditioned to threes. Example: “We serve lasagna, spaghetti, linguini, and poi.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of setup — eliminate ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be very careful that the first two items clearly establish the pattern you’re setting up. You don’t want the audience to have to work to make the connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the initial items could be read in multiple ways, the payoff will fail. Anti-patterns: “The Giants, Detroit, and the Teamsters.” (murky) Better: “The Giants, the Tigers, and the Teamsters.” Also avoid items like “The Reds, the Blues, and the Teamsters” where the first two could mean politics, teams, or drugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the setup straight — save the funny for the payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: You hurt the punchline if one of the setups is funny. It’s okay that the set up be straight. Save the funny for the payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a ‘joke-on-a-joke’ in the setup because two jokes can cancel each other out. Example of bad setup: “Linda, Moon Unit, and Mother Teresa.” (one setup is already funny)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid convoluted setups — keep it simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t make your set up too convoluted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, complex setups lose the audience before the punchline arrives. Maintain simple, clean phrasing and structure so the punchline lands. Anti-pattern example: an overlong multi-clause description that confuses listeners by the time you reach the payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Think rhythm, think timing. This is comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery, pacing, and the rhythmic expectation of a three-part list are integral to the joke working. Emphasize cadence and timing when writing and performing the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payoff must break the pattern but remain connected
rubrics_metrics.description: The payoff has to break the pattern but not so much so that it’s a non-sequitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punchline should be unexpected yet still tied to the established pattern — not a random non-sequitur. Example: “The Giants, the Tigers, and poi.” (fails because poi doesn't connect at all) The payoff should be surprising but have something that ties it back to the set-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline quality — iterate to find best payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Rule-of-Threes is so familiar, audiences see it coming; extra pressure is placed on your punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to find the strongest version of your payoff; try alternatives and refine wording. Example contrast: “Our fresh fish today is halibut, salmon, or canned tuna” versus “Our fresh fish today is halibut, salmon, and gefilte.” The latter is funnier because of word choice and concept, but be mindful of audience knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity improves comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The more specific in comedy the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, specific details (names, precise objects, odd cultural words) can sharpen the joke and make the payoff funnier. Use specificity to enhance surprise and imagery, but balance with audience familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience — avoid obscure references without context
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to know your audience. If you’re not part of the target audience you might never have heard of a reference, and funny words alone aren’t always enough to get a laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t rely solely on obscure or culturally-specific words (e.g., 'gefilte') unless you’re sure the audience understands the reference. A funny-sounding word can help, but it shouldn’t be the only mechanism for the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation: Stan Daniels’ Turn (inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variation where the punchline is the exact opposite of the first two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversion as a structured variation of the Rule-of‑Threes: set up two similar (usually negative) attributes and finish with an unexpected positive or opposite. Example: “She’s hateful, she’s despicable, I’m in love.” It’s formulaic but effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility of list elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The list doesn't have to be objects or names; it can be words or other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can apply the rule to different kinds of items — objects, names, adjectives, words — so long as the pattern is clear and the payoff breaks it in a connected, surprising way. Example note in post: the list can be words (example given: 'two').
